identity_notes: No retrieved human trial administers isolated free L-isoleucine as a standalone oral supplement at a therapeutic dose with a clean placebo comparison; every kept human RCT/review studies isoleucine only as one component of a combination product — most commonly a branched-chain amino acid (BCAA) blend with leucine and valine (where isoleucine is typically the smallest fraction, e.g., 250 mg of a 1000 mg capsule, or 1.5 g of a 7.5 g blend), or as part of a bioactive di/tripeptide (isoleucine-tryptophan; isoleucine-proline-proline/IPP paired with valine-proline-proline/VPP) embedded in a dairy or whey-protein-hydrolysate food matrix. The single most important applicability caveat: because isoleucine is essentially never tested in isolation, no finding in this evidence base can be confidently attributed to isoleucine specifically rather than to leucine (typically the dominant, most-studied BCAA) or to the combination as a whole — this is true even for the one exception, PMID 33310174, where an isolated 10 g isoleucine arm was compared directly against leucine and control, and found NO benefit on the primary glycemic outcome in type 2 diabetes. The evidence base is overwhelmingly dominated (over 85% of records) by observational metabolomics/biomarker-discovery studies across dozens of diseases (cancer, diabetes, cardiovascular disease, stroke, lupus, endometriosis, etc.) in which isoleucine is measured only as one of many circulating metabolites and is never administered, plus a large cluster of inborn-error-of-metabolism disease case reports/reviews (methylmalonic acidemia, maple syrup urine disease, 3-ketothiolase/beta-ketothiolase deficiency, ECHS1 deficiency) concerning isoleucine catabolism disorders requiring dietary restriction rather than supplementation.
